newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Assassins execute Taiwan magistrate, seven others.
newsitem.headline: Assassins execute Taiwan magistrate, seven others.

text.p: Assassins burst into a county magistrate's home, tied up nine people and shot each in the head on Thursday, methodically executing the official and seven others in one of Taiwan's most sensational crimes in memory.
The only surviving victim was in critical condition with only weak vital signs and unlikely to live, authorities said.
Taoyuan county magistrate Liu Pang-yu, 54, a member of Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party, died in hospital seven hours after the morning shooting, hospital officials said.
Taoyuan police said two gunmen burst into Liu's home, bound the hands of Liu and eight others and systematically shot each in the head at close range. Five died at the scene.
Police declined to comment on possible motives for one of the most horrific crimes to hit Taiwan in years.
Liu and two county council members who also died were all elected officials.

The assassination rekindled memories of the February 28, 1980, killing of the mother and daughters of a jailed Taiwan independence advocate in their home in a politically charged case that remains unsolved.

The Justice Ministry in August launched a crackdown on scores of crime gangs that Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao said had infiltrated Taiwan's business and political circles and even parliament, triggering fears of underworld reprisals.
Police said magistrate Liu's killers worked swiftly in what had all the signs of a premeditated assassination.
"The method of the shooting shows that they wanted them to die at once. It took just about 10 minutes," a police spokesman said from Taoyuan, home of Taiwan's main airport south of Taipei.
Investigators found a stolen getaway car abandoned nearby as police mounted a massive search for the killers. The island's air and seaports stepped up checks on all departing passengers.
The Interior Ministry offered a T$3 million (US$109,100) reward for information leading to the assassins' arrest.
The state-run Central News Agency, without citing a source, said the killings could involve a property development case.
Investigators would not rule out a link to Taiwan's rough and tumble politics, newspapers said, while state radio said the killers could have organised crime connections.
Aside from Liu and the two council members, police said the victims included Liu's cousin and staff members -- security guards, a driver, a secretary and a maid.

President Lee Teng-hui's office issued a statement of regret and called for speedy police work. "President Lee is extremely shocked," it said. "He has ordered related government agencies to solve the case as soon as possible."
Evening newspapers splashed grisly pictures of the scene on their front pages and condemned the brazen show of brutality at the home of a senior government official.
"This is a common scene in movies," the China Times Express said in an editorial. "Unfortunately this is no longer just a movie plot but the real situation in Taiwan."
The United Evening News appealed for public faith in an editorial headlined: "Taiwan has become Sicily".
"Don't let the people lose confidence in the government's ability to crack down on crimes," the newspaper said.
